analyst_output.research_question: How does Hyperband improve hyperparameter optimization efficiency compared to Bayesian methods?
analyst_output.paper_overview: The paper introduces **Hyperband**, a novel approach for hyperparameter optimization that frames the problem as an adaptive resource allocation task. Unlike traditional Bayesian Optimization (BO) which assumes smoothness or low effective dimensions, Hyperband uses early stopping on partially trained models to efficiently discard poor configurations while investing more resources in promising ones.
analyst_output.methodology:
1. **Adaptive Resource Allocation**: Instead of training all configurations fully, Hyperband allocates computational budget (e.g., epochs) dynamically.
2. **Early Stopping Strategy**: Poor-performing runs are terminated early based on validation loss trends.
3. **Pure-Exploration Bandit Formulation**: The problem is modeled as an infinite-armed bandit where the goal is to identify good configurations without relying on strong structural assumptions about the objective function.

what_to_know: Hyperband is theoretically grounded in the **infinite-armed bandit** setting.
It avoids assumptions about convergence rates that often fail empirically (unlike parametric methods).
The method scales well because it does not require fitting complex posterior distributions like Gaussian Processes.
Adaptive Allocation**: Exploits situations where adaptive allocation works well while protecting against cases requiring conservative approaches.

The paper distinguishes between the 'finite horizon' setting ($R < \infty$, known convergence point) and the 'infinite horizon' setting ($R = \infty$). Hyperband is analyzed primarily in the infinite-horizon case for theoretical tractability, though finite horizons are more common in practice.
Hyperband dynamically allocates resources by running multiple instances of Successive Halving with different budgets ($B_{k,s} = 2^k, n_{k,s} = 2^s$) and combining their results.
Hyperband addresses the issue of not knowing the optimal $n$ or $B$.
By trying different values in a specific order and doubling the budget, it ensures that the loss from identifying the 'best' setting is no more than $\log(B)$ times necessary.
implementation_details: The function $\gamma(j)$ represents how quickly a model's validation loss converges. If training on full data takes time $T$, then $\gamma(k)=0$ for all $k \ge T$.

On CIFAR-10, state-of-the-art results using more data (including validation set) achieve ~17.0% error vs. our 15.0–18% range depending on setup; this gap is attributed to larger training sets and extended epochs in prior work.
The paper highlights shortcomings in the experimental setup, such as random search testing varying numbers of configurations depending on dataset size.
Some classifiers/preprocessing methods cause memory errors (quadratic storage requirements), which can waste time if a searcher trains on a subsample but fails on the full dataset.
The result highlights a dependency on the maximum of exponents $\beta$ and $\alpha$, modulated by logarithmic factors.

warnings: Consistency Guarantees**: Assumes uniform sampling from hyperparameter space; better priors improve performance.
Cost Trade-off**: Requires approximately (smax + 1) times more work than single-value SuccessiveHalving but removes need for manual n selection.
The paper shows that SuccessiveHalving generally requires less average resource per arm compared to uniform allocation for distinguishing top arms.
Infinite horizon Hyperband underperforms finite version within fixed budgets because it must tune max resource R and starts with less aggressive early stopping.
Hyperband assumes computation scales linearly with data set size; for very small datasets, initialization overheads dominate.
Hyperband is particularly effective when the evaluation of a hyperparameter configuration requires multiple epochs.

# HpBandSter [![Build Status](https://travis-ci.org/automl/HpBandSter.svg?branch=master)](https://travis-ci.org/automl/HpBandSter)  [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/automl/HpBandSter/branch/master/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/automl/HpBandSter)
a distributed Hyperband implementation on Steroids

## News: Not Maintained Anymore!

Please note that we don't maintain this repository anymore. We also cannot ensure that we can reply to issues in the issue tracker or look into PRs. 

We offer two successor  packages which showed in our [HPOBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06716) superior performance:

1. [SMAC3](https://github.com/automl/SMAC3): is a versatile HPO package with different HPO strategies. It also implements the main idea of BOHB, but uses a RF (or GP) as a predictive model instead of a KDE.
2. [DEHB](https://github.com/automl/dehb): is a HPO package using a combination of differential evolution and hyperband. 

In particular, SMAC3 has an active group of developers working on it and maintaining it. So, we strongly recommend using one of these two packages instead of HPBandSter.

## Overview

This python 3 package is a framework for distributed hyperparameter optimization.
It started out as a simple implementation of [Hyperband (Li et al. 2017)](http://jmlr.org/papers/v18/16-558.html), and contains
an implementation of [BOHB (Falkner et al. 2018)](http://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/falkner18a.html)

## How to install

We try to keep the package on PyPI up to date. So you should be able to install it via:
```
pip install hpbandster
```
If you want to develop on the code you could install it via:

```
python3 setup.py develop --user
```

## Documentation

The documentation is hosted on github pages: [https://automl.github.io/HpBandSter/](https://automl.github.io/HpBandSter/)
It contains a quickstart guide with worked out examples to get you started in different circumstances.
Check it out if you are interest in applying one of the implemented optimizers to your problem.

We have also written a [blogpost](https://www.automl.org/blog_bohb/) showcasing the results from our ICML paper.

In particular, SMAC3 has an active group of developers working on it and maintaining it. So, we strongly recommend using one of these two packages instead of HPBandSter.

## Overview

This python 3 package is a framework for distributed hyperparameter optimization.
It started out as a simple implementation of [Hyperband (Li et al. 2017)](http://jmlr.org/papers/v18/16-558.html), and contains
an implementation of [BOHB (Falkner et al. 2018)](http://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/falkner18a.html)

## How to install

We try to keep the package on PyPI up to date. So you should be able to install it via:
```
pip install hpbandster
```
If you want to develop on the code you could install it via:

```
python3 setup.py develop --user
```

Array jobs execute the same source multiple times and are bundled together into one job,
